profiles.title: Saint George and the Dragon
profiles.subject: Saints

overview.text: The OCA’s life presents George as a Christian soldier who refused idolatry, suffered under Diocletian, and was beheaded on April 23, 303. Its title Victory-bearer refers especially to his endurance in martyrdom, not simply military achievement.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening account; execution paragraph; paragraph explaining Victory Bearer

overview.reason: Necessary concise account of a modern published explanation; full prose reproduction rights have not been established.

blocks.text: The selected fifteenth-century Novgorod icon in the Tretyakov Gallery shows George on a white horse striking a serpent with his lance. His cloak and the horse’s movement distinguish this narrative image from standing portraits of the saint in armor.

sourceRefs.locator: File description and displayed historic reproduction

blocks.reason: Necessary English description of the selected historic artwork and its published object metadata; no new theological interpretation.

blocks.text: The OCA recounts the dragon episode as a miracle story: a ruler’s daughter is delivered, the beast is overcome, and people turn to Christ. This is the saint’s received hagiographic narrative; the icon does not establish a contemporary eyewitness record of a dragon.

sourceRefs.locator: Final narrative beginning Of the many miracles worked

blocks.text: St. George parish gives symbolic readings of the dragon as Satan or the persecuting emperor and of the rescued princess as the Church or Empress Alexandra. These alternatives belong to that published explanation; they are not a claim that every painter intended identical details.
